public_rationale: WIRED's March 12, 2024 report describes commercial promotion of AI children's videos, without documenting deceptive photorealistic footage made with the specified tools [e1]. OpenAI's December 9, 2024 Sora release announcement does not establish misuse or exclude earlier use of open-source counterparts [e2]. December 11, 2025 reporting describes fake deportation videos posted after Sora's September 2025 update and discusses creator-payment incentives [e3]. Those later examples cannot establish onset soon after February 18, 2024 [e3]. The evidence does not document an early case connecting the specified tool, deceptive photorealistic footage and advertising purpose, leaving the forecast unresolved [e1, e2, e3].
limitations: “In short order” supplies no exact deadline, but still requires near-term onset.
Failure to find an early qualifying case does not establish that none existed.
The later secondary reporting does not verify the generation tool and advertising monetization for an individual qualifying video.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Soon, scammers will use Sora or open-source counterparts to make photorealistic fake videos just to sell ads.

statement.excerpt: In short order, with Sora or some opensource counterparts that will emerge, scammers will start to make photorealistic fake videos simply to sell ads.
statement.document_title: Absolutely amazing ant video augurs intellectual mayhem

from_speaker: with Sora or some opensource counterparts that will emerge
our_interpretation: The forecast concerns deceptive operators publishing realistic-looking fabricated footage to earn advertising income, including platform payouts. It does not require a criminal conviction or proof that profit was their only private motive.
Photorealistic means footage that an ordinary viewer could plausibly mistake for a recording of real events. AI-written scripts, synthetic narration and obvious cartoons alone do not qualify.
The named technology is Sora or an open-source video-generation counterpart. Evidence identifying only an unspecified AI tool does not establish this element.
The surrounding discussion makes YouTube the main example, without expressly excluding comparable video platforms.

In short order means soon after the February 18, 2024 post. It supplies no defensible last calendar day. No numerical deadline is imposed, and examples nearly two years later cannot establish the near-term timing.
Using the named tools is part of the predicted practice, not a separate conditional antecedent.
criteria.support_condition: Dated records establish that, shortly after the post, deceptive operators began publishing photorealistic fabricated videos made with Sora or an open-source counterpart for advertising income. The records must connect the videos, generation tool, deceptive presentation and commercial purpose.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reliable evidence establishes that the specified practice did not begin within the near-term period meant by the claim. Missing examples in a search, or Sora's release date alone, cannot establish this. A deadline chosen by the evaluator cannot justify contradiction.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Dated records of a qualifying case unambiguously soon after February 18, 2024, connecting published videos, Sora or an open-source counterpart, deceptive photorealism, and advertising income or documented intent to obtain it. Reliable evidence establishing that the practice did not begin in that near-term period could settle the claim negatively; search silence alone cannot.
